The Cell Cycle: Phases and Regulation

blocks.x: The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its contents and divides into two daughter cells. It is broadly divided into interphase (the growth and preparation period) and M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis). Interphase itself occupies the vast majority of the cycle — roughly 90% of the total cell cycle time in a typical dividing cell — while M phase is comparatively brief. The correct order of phases is:

items: G1 (Gap 1): The cell grows in size, synthesizes RNA and proteins, and produces organelles needed for DNA replication. This is when the cell size effectively doubles in preparation for division. Rates of RNA transcription and protein synthesis are high in G1, in contrast to S phase.

S (Synthesis): DNA replication occurs; each chromosome is duplicated to form two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. DNA polymerase is active during S phase. Interestingly, during S phase the overall rates of RNA transcription and general protein synthesis fall to very low levels compared with G1/G2, as cellular machinery is redirected toward genome duplication. Chromatin replicates in a defined temporal order: gene-rich, lightly staining euchromatin (including G-bands as visualized differently, but classically G-bands replicate in the second half of S phase while R-bands/euchromatin replicate earlier) — a fact tested directly in some quizzes ("G-bands replicate in the second half of the S phase").

G2 (Gap 2): The cell continues to grow and synthesizes proteins required for mitosis, such as tubulins for spindle formation. Chromosome condensation and microtubule (spindle-precursor) assembly begin during G2, even before visible prophase condensation. G2 ends with the G2/M checkpoint, and cells committing to division carry inactive M-CDK (in complex with cyclin B) in large amounts at the end of G2, ready for rapid activation.
M (Mitotic) phase: Nuclear division (mitosis: prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) followed by cytokinesis, the physical splitting of the cytoplasm into two cells.

G0: A quiescent, non-dividing state that cells can enter from G1. Cells in G0 have exited the active cycle but retain the ability to re-enter G1 when stimulated (e.g., by growth factors or wound signals) — "cells in the G0 phase may re-enter the G1 phase" is a true statement often tested. Terminally differentiated cells (e.g., most neurons and cardiac muscle cells) remain permanently in G0. Notably, nerve cells of mammals have the longest interphase of any cell type, since many stay arrested in G0/G1 for the organism's lifetime. By contrast, cancer cells generally fail to enter (or escape) G0, continuing to cycle inappropriately due to loss of growth control.

blocks.x: Cell division is essential for growth, tissue repair/regeneration, and asexual reproduction in eukaryotes; mitosis in particular underlies wound healing and regeneration. Of the roughly 22,000 genes in a human cell, an estimated ~600 genes are thought to play a direct role in mitosis.

Progression through the cycle is driven by cyclical activation and inactivation of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), whose activity requires binding to regulatory subunits called cyclins. Cyclin concentrations rise and fall at characteristic points of the cycle (cyclins were first discovered in sea urchin embryos, though detailed molecular dissection of cell-cycle control has been carried out extensively in yeast, especially fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe and budding yeast). Depending on the exam framing, cyclins are sometimes described as accumulating across G1, S, and G2 (i.e., "all of these" phases), since different cyclin-CDK pairs peak at different times: G1 cyclins, G1/S cyclins, S-phase cyclins, and mitotic (M-phase) cyclins.
MPF / M-CDK
Maturation-Promoting Factor (MPF), also called M-phase promoting factor or M-CDK, is the complex of cyclin B and Cdc2 (CDK1) that triggers entry into mitosis.

items: Inactive M-CDK (cyclin B bound to phosphorylated, inactive Cdc2) accumulates in large amounts at the end of G2 phase.

Cdc25 is a protein phosphatase that removes inhibitory phosphate groups from Cdc2, thereby dephosphorylating and activating M-CDK. Cdc25 itself is phosphorylated (and kept in check) throughout much of interphase but becomes active as the cell approaches mitosis.

Once activated, MPF/active M-CDK induces essentially all the hallmark events of mitotic entry: breakdown of the nuclear envelope, condensation of chromosomes, and assembly of the mitotic spindle ("all of these" is the correct composite answer on this point).

Exit from mitosis requires MPF inactivation: ubiquitin-mediated cyclin B degradation (via the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, APC/C) destroys cyclin, inactivating Cdc2. The resulting fall in MPF activity initiates anaphase and leads to chromosome decondensation, chromosome segregation, nuclear envelope reformation, and cytokinesis — again, "all of these" together.
Cyclin is characteristically destroyed during every mitosis, only to be resynthesized in the next cycle.

blocks.x: The Three Major Checkpoints

items: G1/S checkpoint (restriction point): Assesses cell size, nutrient availability, and DNA integrity before committing to replication. The retinoblastoma protein (pRb) normally sequesters the E2F transcription factor, blocking S-phase genes; growth-factor signaling leads to CDK-mediated phosphorylation of Rb, releasing E2F and allowing S-phase entry.

G2/M checkpoint: Confirms that DNA replication is complete and undamaged before allowing mitotic entry. In yeast, the rad9 gene is a classic example of a checkpoint gene that delays mitotic entry of G2 cells when DNA damage is detected, giving the cell time to repair before dividing.

Spindle-assembly (metaphase) checkpoint: Ensures all chromosomes are correctly attached to spindle microtubules via their kinetochores before anaphase is allowed to proceed, preventing missegregation.

blocks.x: Tumour Suppressors: p53, p21, Rb

items: p53 is a transcription factor and tumour suppressor often called the "Guardian of the Genome." In a normal, undamaged cell, p53 protein levels are kept low through continuous degradation, primarily regulated by its major negative regulator, Mdm2 (an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for destruction). Upon DNA damage, p53 is stabilized and activates transcription of downstream genes (it is a transcriptional activator, not an anti-transcriptional one). p53 functions to delay entry of cells with damaged DNA into S phase, providing time for repair or, if damage is irreparable, triggering apoptosis.

p21 is a downstream target of p53: it is a CDK inhibitor protein that binds to cyclin-CDK complexes and blocks entry into S phase, distinguishing it from p53 itself (p53 is the upstream sensor/transcription factor; p21 is the effector protein that binds CDK directly).
pRb (retinoblastoma protein) and p53 are both classic tumour-suppressor proteins; loss-of-function mutations in either predispose to cancer.

ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated) encodes a protein kinase that also acts as a tumour suppressor; it senses double-strand DNA breaks and, among other effects, prevents the separation of centrioles as part of enforcing cell-cycle arrest after DNA damage.

Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF) is a small, single-polypeptide-chain protein that stimulates cell proliferation by binding cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases and triggering downstream signaling cascades that push cells through G1.

blocks.x: Clinical note: Circulating red blood cells are normally enucleate and do not divide; a circulating RBC that retains a nucleus/chromosome (or otherwise shows evidence of active division) can be a warning sign of a red-cell cancer/dysplasia.
Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter nuclei, each with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. It is conventionally divided into five stages plus cytokinesis:

items: Prophase: Chromatin condenses and chromosomes first become visible as discrete structures under the light microscope (note that condensation actually begins molecularly back in G2, but becomes visually obvious in prophase). The mitotic spindle begins to assemble from the two centrosomes, which migrate toward opposite poles. The nucleolus disappears and, toward the end of prophase, the nuclear envelope begins to break down.
Prometaphase: The nuclear envelope fully breaks down; kinetochores assemble on centromeres and spindle microtubules attach to them, beginning to move chromosomes toward the cell's equator.

Metaphase: All chromosomes' centromeres line up along the metaphase plate (equator) of the cell, each attached to spindle fibers from both poles. This is the classic stage used to count/photograph chromosomes (karyotyping) because condensation is maximal and chromosomes are aligned.

Anaphase: The centromere of each chromosome divides, separating sister chromatids, which are pulled to opposite poles by shortening spindle microtubules. Anaphase is typically the shortest stage of mitosis. The fall in MPF activity is what initiates this transition.
Telophase: Chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes reform around each set of chromosomes, and nucleoli reappear.

Cytokinesis: Division of the cytoplasm into two daughter cells. In animal cells this occurs via a contractile actomyosin ring that pinches the cell in two, leaving a transient connecting structure called the midbody at the end of cytokinesis. In plant cells, which have rigid walls, cytokinesis instead proceeds by centrifugal formation of a cell plate that grows outward from the center of the cell to the periphery.

blocks.x: Throughout mitosis, each chromosome behaves independently of the others (unlike the paired behavior of homologs in meiosis I). A cell with 40 chromosomes entering mitosis still has 40 chromosomes during anaphase (chromatid separation doubles the chromosome count transiently to 80 "chromosomes," by strict definition once chromatids separate they become independent chromosomes—but many exam keys treat this as remaining "40" if just before full separation; check your course's convention, though most contemporary biology keys count post-anaphase chromatids as 40 chromosomes per pole, i.e., 80 total in the cell). Kinetochores are protein structures assembled on centromeres that serve as attachment sites for spindle microtubules (not themselves forming the spindle). Motor proteins kinesin and dynein associate with spindle apparatus components and generate opposing forces along microtubules to help organize and move chromosomes; microtubules running from a given spindle pole to kinetochores share the same polarity. Condensin is a multi-subunit protein complex responsible for mitotic chromosome condensation.

Amitosis (direct nuclear division without a visible spindle or distinct mitotic stages, seen in some protozoans and unusual cell types) was not discovered by "Carpenter" — that specific attribution is false on relevant exam items. An unusual variant, endomitosis/polyteny, occurs in the salivary gland cells of Drosophila, where somatic pairing of homologous chromosomes occurs (forming giant polytene chromosomes) — an exception to the general rule that homolog pairing is restricted to meiosis.

Meiosis is the specialized division that produces haploid gametes (or spores) from a diploid germ cell, via one round of DNA replication followed by two successive divisions (meiosis I and meiosis II) — not two replication cycles, a common point of confusion tested directly ("two replication cycles of DNA are followed by two divisions" is false).
Meiosis I (reductional division) — homologs separate
Prophase I is markedly longer and more complex than mitotic prophase, and is subdivided into five substages:

items: Leptotene: Chromosomes begin to condense and become visible as long, thin threads.

Zygotene: Homologous chromosomes begin synapsis — pairing side by side, mediated by the synaptonemal complex (a proteinaceous, zipper-like structure that holds homologs in tight alignment). Each paired unit is a bivalent (or tetrad, referring to the four chromatids present). The observation that each such pairing involves exactly one paternal and one maternal chromosome was first described by Montgomery (1901).

Pachytene: Chromosomes are fully synapsed; bivalents (tetrads) are clearly visible, and this is the stage during which crossing over (reciprocal exchange of DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes) physically occurs, producing the recombinant DNA molecules that will later be visible as chiasmata. This is also frequently the longest-duration substage, sometimes lasting days, weeks, or even years (e.g., in human oocytes, which can remain arrested near this stage for decades).

Diplotene: The synaptonemal complex disassembles and homologs begin to separate slightly, but remain held together at chiasmata (the visible sites of prior crossing-over). This is the stage in which separation of homologous chromosomes formally begins. Diplotene can be extremely prolonged — in human female oocytes, diplotene arrest can last from before birth until ovulation decades later, so "diplotene may last for months or years" is true.

Diakinesis: Chromosomes condense maximally; bivalents appear as darkly stained, round/compact bodies and chiasmata become nearly fully terminalised (moved toward chromosome ends) as homologs prepare for alignment. Note that full terminalisation of chiasmata is more classically associated with metaphase I in some texts, so watch for exact question wording.

blocks.x: Following prophase I: in metaphase I, bivalents (not individual chromosomes) align at the equator, with homologous pairs oriented so that each homolog faces a different pole. In anaphase I, whole homologous chromosomes (each still consisting of two sister chromatids) separate from each other and move to opposite poles — this is the "disjunction" step, and centromeres do not divide at this point. In telophase I nuclear envelopes may reform (variably) around each haploid-but-still-duplicated chromosome set, followed by cytokinesis.
Meiosis II (equational division) — sister chromatids separate

Meiosis II closely resembles a mitotic division, but operating on a haploid cell: prophase II, metaphase II (chromosomes align singly at the equator), anaphase II (centromeres finally divide and sister chromatids separate, becoming independent chromosomes), and telophase II followed by cytokinesis. The final products are four haploid cells (in males) or one egg plus polar bodies (in females). Note that "separation of chromosomes into (component) chromatids" is specifically an anaphase II event, distinguishing it from anaphase I (homolog separation).

Some organisms show notable variations: in certain insect groups (e.g., male Diptera such as Drosophila), meiosis proceeds without a synaptonemal complex and without any crossing over in males (achiasmate meiosis) — though a small amount of male crossing over has been reported in some other Diptera species, such as D. malerkotliana. In Odonata (dragonflies), the interval between the two meiotic divisions is compressed such that telophase I and the following interphase are omitted entirely, proceeding directly from anaphase I into meiosis II.
In humans, mature but unfertilized secondary oocytes are arrested at metaphase II (not "meiosis III," which does not exist), completing meiosis II only upon fertilization.

sections.title: Sources of Genetic Variation and the 2^n Rule

blocks.x: Meiosis generates genetic diversity through two independent mechanisms: (1) crossing over in prophase I, which recombines alleles along a chromosome, and (2) independent assortment of homologous chromosome pairs during metaphase I, which randomizes which maternal or paternal homolog of each pair ends up in a given gamete. For an organism heterozygous at n independently assorting gene loci (on different chromosome pairs), the number of genetically distinct gamete types possible from independent assortment alone is 2n. For example, a trihybrid (heterozygous at 3 loci) can produce 23 = 8 distinct gamete types with respect to those three genes. This 2^n rule is distinct from (and multiplies with) the additional variation contributed by crossing over.
Both processes begin with diploid germ cells undergoing mitotic proliferation followed by meiosis, but they differ substantially in outcome:

items: Spermatogenesis: A diploid spermatogonium enlarges into a primary spermatocyte, which completes meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes, each of which completes meiosis II to yield a total of four equal-sized, functional haploid spermatids that mature (spermiogenesis) into motile sperm. All four products are functional gametes.

Oogenesis: A diploid oogonium develops into a primary oocyte, which undergoes highly asymmetric cytoplasmic division. Meiosis I yields one large secondary oocyte and a small, non-functional first polar body (which may or may not divide further). The secondary oocyte proceeds into meiosis II but arrests at metaphase II until fertilization; upon fertilization it completes meiosis II asymmetrically to produce one large fertilized egg (ovum) and a second small polar body. Net result: one functional egg and up to three polar bodies per primary oocyte, concentrating nearly all cytoplasm and nutrient stores in the single viable gamete.

blocks.x: This asymmetry ensures the egg retains sufficient cytoplasmic resources (mitochondria, mRNAs, nutrients) to support early embryonic development, while sperm are optimized for numbers and motility instead.
